procedural_history.impugned_order: Order by the Magistrate directing the police to submit a charge-sheet against the petitioners/appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioners challenged the Magistrate's order before the Sessions Judge, Bhagalpur, and then the Patna High Court, both without success. The Patna High Court, following its previous decision, held that the Magistrate had jurisdiction to call for a charge-sheet when he disagrees with the report submitted by the police.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners challenged the orders of the Magistrate and the High Court in the Supreme Court, arguing that the Magistrate has no jurisdiction to direct the police to file a charge-sheet when the police have submitted a final report stating that no case is made out.

directions: The orders of the Magistrate, directing the police to file a charge, will be set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate has the jurisdiction to direct the police to submit a charge-sheet when the police, after investigation, have submitted a final report under Section 169 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating that no case is made out for sending the accused for trial.

law.fact_text: The Code of Criminal Procedure outlines distinct and separate functions for the police and the Magistracy.

The final step of a police investigation is the formation of an opinion by the police as to whether a case is made out to place the accused on trial. This function is to be performed only by the police and no other authority.
The submission of a charge-sheet (under s. 170) or a final report (under s. 169) is entirely dependent on the opinion formed by the police at the conclusion of their investigation.
The Code of Criminal Procedure does not contain any express or implied power that allows a Magistrate to compel the police to submit a charge-sheet.

A Magistrate has other powers when presented with a final report: they can accept it and close the case; order a further investigation under s. 156(3) if the initial one seems incomplete; or take cognizance of the offense themselves under s. 190(1)(c) if they disagree with the police's conclusion.

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that directing the police to submit a charge-sheet would mean compelling them to change their opinion, which is formed at the end of their investigation. This would be an infringement upon the jurisdiction of the police.

The Court used a logical analogy: if the police submit a charge-sheet, a Magistrate cannot compel them to submit a final report instead. It follows, therefore, that the Magistrate also cannot compel the police to submit a charge-sheet when they have filed a final report.

The Court emphasized that the Magistrate is not powerless. Instead of ordering the police to change their report, the Magistrate can use their own judicial powers. If they suspect an offense has been committed despite the police's final report, they can take cognizance of the offense under Section 190(1)(c) and proceed with the case.

The existence of these alternative legal pathways for the Magistrate (like ordering further investigation or taking cognizance independently) reinforces the conclusion that there is no need for an implied power to order the police to file a charge-sheet.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Magistrate has no power, either expressly or impliedly conferred under the Code of Criminal Procedure, to direct the police to submit a charge-sheet when the police have already submitted a final report stating that no case is made out for sending the accused to trial. The formation of an opinion on the investigation is the exclusive sphere of the police, and while a Magistrate can disagree with that opinion and take other actions, they cannot compel the police to change it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate has the jurisdiction to direct the police to submit a charge-sheet when the police, after investigation, have submitted a final report under Section 169 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating that no case is made out for sending the accused for trial.
appellant_arguments: When the police submit a final report stating that no case is made out, the Magistrate has no jurisdiction to direct the police to file a charge-sheet.

The formation of an opinion on whether there is a case to place the accused on trial is the responsibility of the investigating officers, and the Magistrate cannot compel the police to form a particular opinion.

The Magistrate has other legal options, such as directing further investigation or treating a protest petition as a formal complaint and taking cognizance of the offense, but cannot directly order the submission of a charge-sheet.
respondent_arguments: A Magistrate has the jurisdiction to direct the police to submit a charge-sheet when they disagree with the final report submitted by the police.
If the Magistrate does not have this power, the entire matter would be left to the sole discretion of the police.

statutes.act_name: The Code (presumably the Code of Criminal Procedure)

cases.case_name: State of West Bengal v. S. N. Basak

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate has no jurisdiction to direct the police to submit a charge-sheet. The formation of an opinion as to whether or not there is a case to place an accused on trial is a function left to the police under the Code, and a Magistrate cannot compel the police to form a particular opinion on the investigation and submit a report according to that opinion, as this would be an encroachment on the sphere of the police.
obiter: When a Magistrate disagrees with a police report that states no case is made out, the Magistrate may direct further investigation.
When a Magistrate disagrees with a police report that states no case is made out, the Magistrate may treat a protest petition as a complaint and take cognizance of the offense.

When a Magistrate disagrees with a police report that states no case is made out, the Magistrate can take cognizance of the offense under s. 190(1)(c) if they form the opinion that the facts in the report constitute an offense.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Magistrate cannot direct the police to submit a charge-sheet when the police have filed a final report finding no case. The submission of a report is dependent entirely upon the opinion formed by the police based on their investigation, and a Magistrate cannot compel the police to form a particular opinion. While a Magistrate has supervisory powers and is not bound by the police report, their recourse upon disagreement is to take cognizance of the offense themselves under Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or to order further investigation, not to command the investigating agency to file a charge-sheet against their own conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of separation of functions between the police and the judiciary under the Criminal Procedure Code, where the police are responsible for investigation and the formation of an opinion, and the judiciary's function begins when a charge is preferred before it.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the appellant's arguments, leading to the respondent's loss. The reasoning is as follows:
The submission of a police report depends entirely upon the opinion formed by the police and not on the opinion of the magistrate.
A magistrate cannot compel the police to form a particular opinion on investigation and submit a report according to such opinion.
If a magistrate disagrees with the report of the police, they can take cognizance of the offence themselves under s. 190(1)(a) or (c), which is the proper legal recourse.
The functions of the judiciary and the police are complementary, not overlapping, and the court's functions begin when a charge is preferred before it, and not until then.
policy_considerations: It is of the utmost importance that the judiciary should not interfere with the police in matters which are within their province and into which the law imposes on them the duty of inquiry.
The combination of individual liberty with a due observance of law and order is only to be obtained by leaving each [the judiciary and the police] to exercise its own function.

The power for a magistrate to take cognizance under s. 190(1)(c) was intended to secure that offences may not go unpunished and justice may be invoked even when persons individually aggrieved are unwilling or unable to prosecute, or the police either wantonly or through a bona fide error do not submit a charge-sheet.
